common_name: Rowallane Flowering Quince (Low Spreading Scarlet AGM Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in ordinary, well-drained garden soil in full sun to partial shade; Rowallane is a low, spreading grower named for the garden in Northern Ireland where it originated, and it tolerates poor soil better than most flowering shrubs.

directions: Rowallane holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit for its dependable show of bright scarlet-red, cup-shaped flowers clustered along bare thorny stems in early to mid spring, ahead of most garden shrubs. It grows into a wide, low, spreading mound rather than an upright bush, which makes it a useful choice for softening a bank, low wall, or slope where a taller quince would look out of scale. Small green fruit ripening to yellow follows the bloom and can be simmered into jelly if gathered before frost. Grow in full sun to light shade in any well-drained soil, and shape by cutting back the previous year's growth by about half right after flowering, since blooms form on old wood.

common_name: Nivalis Flowering Quince (Pure White Vigorous Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Nivalis is a large, vigorous white-flowered selection of the Chinese species and needs more room than compact modern quince cultivars.

directions: Nivalis is an old, vigorous flowering quince selection valued for petals of the purest white, opening around a small green eye in dense clusters on thorny, tangled bare branches in early spring, a cooler contrast to the reds and pinks typical of the species. It grows considerably larger and wider than most named quince cultivars, eventually forming a tall, dense, thorny mass well suited to a boundary hedge, screen, or informal barrier planting rather than a small foundation bed. Fragrant yellow-green fruit follows the flowers and can be cooked into preserves. Grow in full sun for the heaviest bloom in any well-drained soil, and prune only right after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds.

common_name: Elly Mossel Flowering Quince (Vivid Crimson-Red Golden-Stamened Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in ordinary, well-drained garden soil in full sun to partial shade; Elly Mossel forms a dense, rounded, thorny bush and can also be trained flat against a wall or fence as an informal espalier.

directions: Elly Mossel produces large, single, vivid crimson-red flowers packed with bright golden-yellow stamens, clustered thickly along bare, thorny stems in early spring for a fiery, high-contrast display. The rounded, dense shrub responds well to training flat against a sunny wall or fence, in addition to standing as a freestanding specimen or informal barrier hedge. Fragrant yellow fruit follows in autumn and can be cooked into jam or jelly. Grow in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering since the buds for next year's bloom set on the current season's wood.

common_name: Rubra Grandiflora Flowering Quince (Large Red Yellow-Stamened Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rubra Grandiflora is a long-lived older cultivar whose new spring foliage emerges reddish before turning dark green.

directions: Rubra Grandiflora bears cup-shaped red flowers centered with bright yellow stamens along its thorny, bare branches in early spring, a large-flowered older selection of the Chinese species that has stayed in cultivation for its reliability. New leaves unfurl with a reddish flush in spring before settling into dark green for the rest of the season, and showy yellow pomes appear by mid fall. It is an unusually long-lived shrub, often persisting for decades in the same spot with minimal care once established. Grow in full sun in any well-drained soil, and prune only immediately after flowering to preserve next year's bloom, which forms on older wood.

common_name: Colorita Claressa Alstroemeria (Compact Continuous-Blooming Peruvian Lily)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Claressa belongs to the compact, triploid Colorita series bred by Royal Van Zanten in the Netherlands for extended garden and container bloom.

directions: Claressa is a compact selection from the triploid Colorita breeding line, producing a long, dense succession of flowers from spring through autumn rather than the shorter single flush typical of older Alstroemeria strains. Its naturally tidy, well-branched habit keeps it in scale for patio containers and border edges without staking. Spent stems should be pulled firmly from the base rather than cut, which triggers fresh flowering shoots from the crown and keeps the display going for months. In marginal zones mulch heavily over winter or lift and store the roots, and divide crowded clumps in early spring every few years to keep vigor up.

common_name: Colorita Yentl Alstroemeria (Compact Continuous-Blooming Peruvian Lily)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Yentl belongs to the compact, triploid Colorita series bred by Royal Van Zanten in the Netherlands for extended garden and container bloom.

directions: Yentl is a compact Colorita-series selection bred for a long, repeat-flowering season that runs from spring into fall rather than a single short spring flush. The dense, well-proportioned habit suits containers, patio beds, and the front of a mixed border alike, staying in scale without support. Pull rather than cut faded flower stems from the base to prompt new shoots and prolong bloom, and treat it as marginally hardy outside its recommended zones, mulching heavily or lifting tubers for winter storage where freezes are severe. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to renew flowering vigor.

common_name: Colorita Katiana Alstroemeria (Compact Continuous-Blooming Peruvian Lily)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Katiana belongs to the compact, triploid Colorita series bred by Royal Van Zanten in the Netherlands for extended garden and container bloom.

directions: Katiana carries the compact habit and long repeat bloom common to the Colorita series, sending up successive flowering stems over many weeks instead of one short seasonal peak. Its restrained size keeps it well-suited to patio pots and small border spaces where larger cutting-garden Alstroemeria would sprawl. As with other Colorita types, pull spent stems from the base rather than shearing them, which encourages the crown to keep producing new flowering shoots. Provide winter protection or lift tubers where the ground freezes hard, and refresh crowded plantings by dividing in early spring every few seasons.

common_name: Little Miss Zoe Alstroemeria (Dwarf Variegated-Foliage Peruvian Lily)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Little Miss Zoe is a patented dwarf selection from the Little Miss breeding line raised by Bob Goemans, notable for cream-edged variegated foliage.

directions: Little Miss Zoe stays noticeably low and dense, its cream-margined variegated foliage offering ornamental interest even before flowering begins, then topped with clusters of colorful blooms typical of the dwarf Little Miss breeding line. Its diminutive scale suits small pots, edging, and rock-garden-style plantings where full-size Alstroemeria would overwhelm the space. Pull entire spent flower stems from the base rather than cutting them, which prompts the crown to send up fresh flowering shoots and extends the bloom season. Protect containers from hard freezes, and where marginally hardy, mulch heavily over the crown or lift and store the roots for winter.
